title: The Small Interior
premise: Hazel Almeida, a night librarian who has spent thirty years cataloguing silences instead of speaking them, finds a box of undelivered letters hidden behind his late mother's wardrobe—letters she wrote to him and never sent, alongside correspondence revealing he had an older brother given away before Hazel was born. As the city's endless noise closes in and his mother's dementia-era notes dissolve into fragments, Hazel must travel back to the coastal town of Vessan where the family fractured, confronting the brother, Tomas, who believes Hazel was the reason he was sent away. The novel ends with Hazel choosing to read one letter aloud at his mother's graveside, delivering thirty years of silence in a single voice, and discovering that belonging is not inherited but built—one unsaid thing finally said.
about_author: Ansel Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed personal effects in municipal storage. They write quietly devastating fiction about the objects people leave behind and the words they never manage to say.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Hazel works the night shift at the Meridian Library, narrating his habit of recording everything he fails to say in a private ledger. A call about his mother's emptied apartment interrupts his routine. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the comfort of invisibility beginning to feel like suffocation.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Clearing the apartment, Hazel pries loose a panel behind his mother's wardrobe and finds a shoebox: dozens of unsent letters addressed to him, plus older ones to someone named 'T.' He reads only the first before fleeing to the library. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: vertigo—the discovery that his careful solitude was built on a hidden architecture.

chapters.title: Letters in Reverse Order
chapters.summary: Hazel reads the letters out of sequence, assembling a mother he never knew: her guilt, her tenderness, her fear. The library's day staff begin noticing his unraveling. POV: Hazel, with interpolated letter fragments. Emotional beat: grief complicated by anger—he was loved, secretly, uselessly.

chapters.title: The Brother in the Margins
chapters.summary: A genealogy request at the reference desk leads Hazel to confirm Tomas Almeida exists, alive, running a boatyard in Vessan. His ledger entries grow erratic as duty (the estate, the funeral arrangements) collides with longing. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the first pull toward departure.

chapters.title: What the City Keeps
chapters.summary: Hazel delays, burying himself in shifts and a tentative friendship with Odile, the morning librarian who has always waited for him to speak. She challenges him gently: 'You archive yourself like you're already gone.' POV: Hazel with a brief Odile passage. Emotional beat: love offered against his instinct for duty to the dead.

chapters.title: Vessan, Off Season
chapters.summary: Hazel takes the coast train to Vessan, a town shrunk by time, and finds the house where the family broke. He watches Tomas from a distance for two days, unable to approach, learning the rhythms of a life that might have been his. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Boatyard
chapters.summary: Hazel finally introduces himself; Tomas receives the news coldly—he knew of Hazel, believed their mother chose to keep him and give Tomas away. A bitter confrontation ends with Tomas telling Hazel to leave. POV: alternating Hazel and Tomas. Emotional beat: the story's central wound exposed from both sides.

chapters.title: The Letter That Was Never Sent
chapters.summary: Among the final letters Hazel finds the one explaining the truth: it was their father's doing, and their mother's silence was shame, not preference. He brings it to Tomas, who refuses to read it alone. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: rising tension breaking toward honesty—two men reading their mother's voice together.

chapters.title: Graveside
chapters.summary: At the burial plot above Vessan harbor, Hazel reads the last letter aloud, delivering decades of unsent words while Tomas listens. The brothers argue, weep, and do not fully reconcile—but something is handed over. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: climax; speech replacing inventory, inheritance redefined as shared rather than divided.

chapters.title: Catalogue of Said Things
chapters.summary: Back in the city, Hazel begins a new ledger listing what he actually says each day. He tells Odile the whole story over coffee, applies to keep the family house open summers, and mails Tomas a postcard with no apology, just an address. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: quiet resolution—belonging chosen, love practiced, silence ended.
